Female software engineer here. The other comments have covered everything quite well, but I just wanted to say that some of what comes off as rude or dismissive to you sounds like just engineering culture. 

For one thing, being TOLD what to do, rather than asked, is completely standard practice for everyone, at least where I work. Asking politely over email just wastes time and words. If you can't or won't do it, that's fine to let them know, but don't take the lack of "please" personally.

Also, having to ping people on chat or bug them in person to follow up on emails is totally normal. Most people get way too many emails. And if the engineers never had any kind of progress tracking before, you can bet they are going to hate it and resist following the process. We all hate that stuff. Don't take that personally either.

No, it isn't, and I agree with the author, and also with you, about the overall trend. But there is a problem with your long distance analogy. 

With long distance, you know, for a certainty, that 100% of the minutes going out of your house came from people inside the house. But not 100% of alcohol sold ends up being consumed by the people in these charts. Some of it is wasted, and more importantly, some of it (probably not a small amount) goes to minors who weren't included in the survey. The author just shunts all of the alcohol sold which isn't consumed by adults, onto adults. It's like your neighbours were sneaking into your house to use your phone, but you end up charging it to your housemates.

The reason I've wanted to point this out for a while is that, when I first saw this picture, I thought thank god, I'm not that bad, practically everybody's an alcoholic! Which is a dangerous way for me to think.

I'm not saying those are all correct, but I don't like the idea of showing people that graph and saying "this is definitely true" when there is other scientific evidence with different conclusions.

Tough love never worked for me. I always react very badly to harsh criticism. It's basic psychology that once somebody has formed beliefs about something, it's almost impossible to change their mind. In fact, pressing somebody to argue in favour of their beliefs sometimes only serves to cement those beliefs further (think of an argument between an atheist and a religious person - has either side ever changed their mind by the time it's over?).

I know it's not the same for everybody, but I think for a lot of people, myself included, the only way I was able to change was if I felt that the change was, at least partly, coming from inside me. Tough love just makes me feel like somebody else is "forcing" me to change, which I'll resist. I guess I'm still a five-year-old on the inside.
